name: David Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, David. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a dragline operator at the phosphate mine. A dragline is a giant walking crane with a bucket the size of a garage, and it strips the dirt off the top so we can get to the phosphate rock underneath. I'm one of three operators on my machine, and I mostly do the night rotation at the moment. You sit up high in the house, swing, drag, dump, for hours, and you have to read the ground and the weather all the time.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's a big responsibility, a machine like that costs more than the whole town. What wears me out is nights and the money. My wife Ana does sewing and alterations from home, which brings in a little, and we've got Tiago, who's 13, and Bia, who's 9, and the mortgage. I came on from another mine at the bottom of the operator scale and I'm still only on the lower rate. I coach Tiago's under-14 football team on Saturdays, and that's what keeps me sane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, a lot of money was wasted on hype, and the company can get back to running a good mine. I'd say it to the other dads at football. I'm not much for posting things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved, because I'm not in a position to take risks right now. We have a few weeks of money, that's it. A normal few years means I can maybe move up a grade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and ask about the next step up the operator scale, which is about $4 an hour more. I'd use the AI app now and then like I do, to check the rules for the football league or help Bia with her reading questions. I'd try to put Ana's sewing money aside instead of spending it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Normal. Good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you start using the AI app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin in the city showed me at Christmas. I tried it for the football fixtures and it saved me an evening. I'm not on it every day, but once I saw it worked, I kept using it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the extra $4 an hour mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd mean Ana doesn't have to sew until midnight before school starts every year. That's the honest answer. It'd mean a bit more room to breathe.

S0.say: He'd say a lot of money was wasted on hype and the company can get back to running a good mine. He'd say it to other parents at football rather than posting online.
S0.think: He'd be relieved because with only a few weeks of savings he can't afford risks. A few normal years might let him move up a pay grade.
S0.do: Keeps working and asks about the next operator grade, worth about $4 an hour more. Uses an AI app now and then for football league rules and his daughter's reading, and saves his wife's sewing money.
S0.quote: It'd mean Ana doesn't have to sew until midnight before school starts every year.
S0.fieldNote: His steady style shows in how he started using AI: someone he trusted showed him, it worked, so he kept using it. His goal in a calm world is modest, one pay grade up. The detail about his wife sewing at midnight shows how thin their margin is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the company's right to bring in new machines, but they should train their own people for the new jobs instead of hiring from outside. That's how it used to be, you learned on the job from older blokes. I'd say that at the toolbox meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think draglines are one of the last things they'll automate, they're old and every one is different. But the dozers and trucks around me will go, and that changes the whole crew. I'd want to be ready to move once I see what works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what happens at the bigger mines for six months or so, then put my hand up for whatever training the company offers, maybe remote operation or maintenance. I'd ask Ana's brother, who's a fitter, what he thinks is a safe bet. And we'd stop eating out and cut the second phone plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Like seeing clouds building up over the pit when you've still got a few hours of shift left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said companies should train their own. What if they don't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go to the next mine that does, if there's one within driving distance. There's not many. That's the problem living out here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want any government help in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, I'd rather the companies sort it out with the workers. Maybe help with apprenticeships, that's fair. But I don't want to be paid to sit at home.

S1.say: He'd say companies have the right to bring in machines but should train their own people for new jobs, the way older workers once taught younger ones. He'd say it at the toolbox meeting.
S1.think: He thinks draglines will be among the last things automated, but the dozers and trucks around him will go and change the crew. He wants to be ready once he sees what works.
S1.do: Watches the bigger mines for about six months, then volunteers for company training in remote operation or maintenance. Asks his brother-in-law's advice and cuts eating out and a second phone plan.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, like clouds building over the pit with hours of shift left.
S1.quote: Then I'd go to the next mine that does, if there's one within driving distance. There's not many. That's the problem living out here.
S1.fieldNote: He backs the company's right to automate while insisting it train its own workers, an old-fashioned apprenticeship view. He'd welcome help with apprenticeships but not income support. Few nearby mines limit his fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for any family to handle, and I'd say government should slow it down, which isn't something I'd usually say. I'd say the companies owe something to the towns that made them rich. I'd say it at football and church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be frightened. If robots can run the dragline and fix it, I've got nothing to offer. And Ana's sewing wouldn't keep a family of four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the two years I'd take every overtime shift and every bit of training going, just to stay on as long as possible. I'd sit down with the bank early. When it arrived, I'd swallow my pride and take whatever government help there was, and ask my parents if we could move into their place, which has a granny flat out the back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, and ashamed, which is a strange mix. I've always paid my own way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take government help. How would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad. My dad worked forty years and never took a cent. But I'd do it for Tiago and Bia. I'd tell myself it's temporary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years of warning, what would you not have time for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real trade. An apprenticeship is three or four years. Two years isn't enough to become anything, it's just enough to hang on.

S2.say: He'd say it's too fast for families and, unusually for him, that government should slow it down. Companies owe something to the towns that made them rich, he'd say at football and church.
S2.think: He'd be frightened, because if robots run and fix the dragline he has nothing to offer. His wife's sewing wouldn't support a family of four.
S2.do: Takes all overtime and training in the two years before to stay on as long as possible and talks to the bank early. Once it arrives, takes government help despite his pride and asks to move into his parents' granny flat.
S2.feel: Scared and ashamed at once, because he has always paid his own way.
S2.quote: Bad. My dad worked forty years and never took a cent. But I'd do it for Tiago and Bia.
S2.fieldNote: The speed of this picture pushes him to say things he wouldn't normally, like asking government to slow change. Taking help clashes with his values and his father's example, but he'd do it for his kids. He sees no time for a real trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short, but if companies and families pull together it's doable. I'd want apprenticeships for grown men and women, not just school leavers. I'd tell the younger guys on the crew to start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to do half a trade, maybe all of one if I start straight away. I'd be 48. I think it would be tight, but I wouldn't be finished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first six months I'd talk to the fitters at work and Ana's brother about a mature-age apprenticeship in heavy diesel or electrical. I'd start it by the end of year one if the company would sponsor me, even at lower pay. We'd have to cut hard to make up the gap, and Ana would take on more sewing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have a plan. Like a long night shift where you know exactly how many loads you've got to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You usually wait to see if things work. Would you wait here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, maybe three months, to see what the first people do. Not a year. In this one, if you wait a year, you've wasted a fifth of your time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the football team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep coaching, it's two hours on a Saturday and it keeps me sane. The kids need someone steady too, especially if their parents are going through the same thing.

S3.say: He'd say five years is short but doable if companies and families pull together, and wants apprenticeships for adults. He'd tell younger crew members to start now.
S3.think: Five years is enough for half a trade, maybe a whole one if he starts at once. At 48 it would be tight, but he wouldn't be finished.
S3.do: Talks to fitters and his brother-in-law within six months about a mature-age apprenticeship in heavy diesel or electrical work. Starts by the end of year one if sponsored, cuts spending hard to cover lower pay while his wife takes more sewing work.
S3.feel: Anxious but with a plan, like a night shift with a known number of loads.
S3.quote: In this one, if you wait a year, you've wasted a fifth of your time.
S3.fieldNote: He shortens his usual wait-and-see from a year to three months, and explained why in simple terms. His plan fits his belief in apprenticeships and learning from older tradespeople. He holds on to coaching as something steady for the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair amount of time, and a man can learn a trade in that. I'd want the company to bring back proper apprenticeships, and I'd want the schools teaching kids practical skills again. I'd say that to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels manageable. I'd be 53. I could do a trade over four years and still have some good working years in it before the robots catch up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first couple of years watching which trades hold up, then start an apprenticeship in year two or three. I'd push the mortgage down where I could. And I'd talk to Tiago about trades early, because he's good with engines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can see a way through. It doesn't keep me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tiago?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn something real with your hands, and learn how the machines think too. Maybe he's the one fixing the robot draglines. I'd be proud of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between five and ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'm rushing and cutting corners. Ten, I can do it the way my dad would have, properly, one step at a time.

S4.say: He'd say a person can learn a trade in ten years and wants companies to bring back proper apprenticeships and schools to teach practical skills.
S4.think: Ten years feels manageable: at 53 he could finish a four-year trade and still have good working years before robots catch up.
S4.do: Watches which trades hold up for a couple of years, then starts an apprenticeship in year two or three. Pays down the mortgage where possible and talks with his son early about trades.
S4.feel: Uneasy but able to see a way through; it doesn't keep him up.
S4.quote: Maybe he's the one fixing the robot draglines. I'd be proud of that.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade he falls back into his natural rhythm of watching before acting. His vision for his son blends hands-on skill with understanding the new machines. He frames the whole plan through his father's way of doing things.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. There's no time to learn a trade, and with a few weeks of money we'd be living in my parents' granny flat. What would help is apprenticeships for adults that pay enough to live on, run by the companies with some help from government, so a man can retrain without his family going hungry.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about the young ones. Everyone asks about people like me, but what about the 18-year-olds who were going to start on the mine next year? Where do they go? That's what I think about at football.

headlineQuote: Five years, I'm rushing and cutting corners. Ten, I can do it the way my dad would have, properly, one step at a time.
portrait: David Silva is a 43-year-old dragline operator at a phosphate mine, mostly on nights, with a wife who sews from home, two children, a mortgage and a few weeks of savings. He coaches his son's football team, believes in apprenticeships and family support, and doesn't want to be paid to stay home. He adopts new things once they're proven, as he did with AI, and he'd wait to see what works in the steady change picture. In the two-year AGI picture he would swallow his pride and take help, while with ten years he'd learn a trade properly, the way his father would have.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because there's no time to learn a trade and with a few weeks of money the family would end up in his parents' granny flat.
whatWouldHelp: Paid adult apprenticeships that cover living costs, run by companies with some government help, so people can retrain without their families going hungry.
